topic: Why almost all data between continents travels through garden-hose-thick fibre-optic cables on the seabed, and how they work

through_line.name: the black seabed cable with a glowing glass core
through_line.progression: the cable is compared with a hose, opened to show its glass strands, fades, gets boosted by repeaters, is laid by a ship and finally outshines a satellite beam
through_line.resolution: the cable returns to the garden and lies beside the hose as in the opening view

blocks.vo_line: Your internet runs through a garden hose. Around ninety-nine percent of data between continents travels in seabed cables about that thick.
blocks.through_line_state: the cable lies beside a garden hose, exactly as thick
shots: CLOSE-UP, static: a garden hose whips across the lawn and blasts a jet of bright light out of its nozzle
LOW ANGLE WIDE, gentle drift: the beam of light arcs over the garden fence toward the sea
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: the black seabed cable drops beside the hose with a thud, the same thickness
OVERHEAD, slow push-in: hose and cable lie side by side on the grass, the cable's cut end glowing
MEDIUM, static: the cable snakes away across the lawn and dives off the garden's edge into the water with a splash

blocks.vo_line: Inside are glass fibres about as thin as a human hair. Lasers flash data through them as pulses of light.
blocks.through_line_state: the cable's cut end opens to show hair-thin glowing glass strands
shots: MEDIUM, gentle drift: the cable settles onto the sandy seabed, puffing up a cloud of sand
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, slow push-in: the cable's cut end peels open layer by layer with a snap, revealing a few thin glowing glass strands
LOW ANGLE WIDE, static: the cable runs off across the sea floor into the blue distance
CLOSE-UP, static: rapid pulses of light race along one glass strand like a string of sparks
HIGH ANGLE MEDIUM, static: the layers close back around the strands and the whole cable glows from within

blocks.vo_line: So why not just beam it through satellites instead? Hold that thought, because light fading in glass is the first problem.
blocks.through_line_state: seen from orbit, the cable's glowing line across the ocean dims as it goes
shots: WIDE, slow orbit: a small satellite swings over the round planet and a dish on it snaps open
CLOSE-UP, static: the satellite sends a thin beam down toward the ocean
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, gentle drift: far below, the cable is a glowing line crossing the blue ocean between two coasts
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: the light pulse inside the cable grows dimmer and dimmer as it travels
MEDIUM, static: the cable's glow fades out halfway across with a soft fizzle

blocks.vo_line: So roughly every forty-five miles, a repeater boosts the light. Its power arrives from shore, thousands of volts through the cable itself.
blocks.through_line_state: a repeater clamps into the cable and the dim light comes out bright again
shots: CLOSE-UP, static: a torpedo-shaped metal repeater clunks into place in the middle of the cable on the sea floor
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, slow push-in: a dim pulse of light enters the repeater and shoots out the other side bright
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, gentle drift: a long row of repeaters along the cable light up one after another into the distance
LOW ANGLE MEDIUM, static: a crackle of electric sparks runs along the cable's skin from the shore side
OVERHEAD, static: the whole cable glows strong and steady across the sand

blocks.vo_line: Ships lay them across entire oceans, some resting miles below the surface. Together they stretch more than nine hundred thousand miles.
blocks.through_line_state: the cable spools off the back of a ship and sinks into the deep
shots: LOW ANGLE MEDIUM, static: a chunky cable ship crashes through a wave, spray flying
CLOSE-UP, static: a giant spool on the deck spins and the cable pays out over the stern
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, crane up: the ship crosses the open ocean trailing the cable into the water behind it
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, gentle drift: the cable sinks down through darkening blue water
WIDE, static: the cable lands on the deep sea floor with a soft thump of sand

blocks.vo_line: Now, those satellites. One Atlantic cable was built for two hundred fifty terabits a second, Google says, far more than any single satellite.
blocks.through_line_state: the cable carries a flood of light while the satellite's beam stays a thin thread
shots: CLOSE-UP, gentle drift: the small satellite drifts along the glowing edge of the planet sending down one thin thread of light
WIDE, static: below it the cable across the ocean swells into a thick bright river of light
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, slow push-in: countless pulses of light pour through the cable's glass strands
HIGH ANGLE MEDIUM, static: the thin thread and the thick river run side by side, and the river surges with a whoosh
LOW ANGLE WIDE, static: the satellite sails on while the cable below blazes from coast to coast

blocks.vo_line: That is why the oceans are mostly wired, not beamed. So the next time a video loads from another continent, remember:
blocks.through_line_state: the cable surfaces back in the garden and lies beside the hose again
shots: MEDIUM, static: the cable bursts up out of the water at the garden's edge with a splash
EXTREME CLOSE-UP, static: its glowing cut end slides across the grass
HIGH ANGLE WIDE, gentle drift: the cable curls through the garden toward the hose
LOW ANGLE CLOSE-UP, static: the cable stops next to the hose with a soft thud
CLOSE-UP, static: hose and cable rest side by side, the hose nozzle glowing gently, settling into the opening view
